title: Ancient 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Misidentified for Decades Finally Revealed by Scientists
body:
A fossil that has long been hailed as a milestone in the early evolution of reptiles has been re‑identified as an entirely different kind of animal, overturning a decades‑old consensus about the origins of land‑dwelling vertebrates. Using high‑resolution synchrotron X‑ray tomography, an international team of paleontologists has uncovered a set of delicate gill structures and thousands of microscopic teeth hidden inside the 345‑million‑year‑old specimen from the Scottish Borders. The findings reveal that the creature was not a reptile at all, but a primitive aquatic or amphibious vertebrate that occupied a niche far removed from the terrestrial lineages previously ascribed to it.

The specimen, originally described in the early 1990s as *Hylonomus* sp., was celebrated for its apparent status as one of the oldest known reptiles, a key piece of evidence for the timing of the reptile‑to‑amphibian transition. At the time, its modest size, elongated body and superficially reptilian vertebrae seemed to fit the emerging picture of early amniotes venturing onto dry land. However, the fossil’s internal anatomy remained largely inaccessible because the rock matrix encasing it is both dense and opaque to conventional imaging methods. The new study employed a synchrotron beam at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, allowing researchers to peer through the limestone without damaging the delicate remains.

What emerged from the scans was a startlingly different portrait. The animal possessed a series of well‑preserved branchial arches—structures that support gills in fish and some early amphibians—indicating that it retained a fully aquatic respiratory system. Even more striking were the thousands of minuscule, needle‑like teeth lining the inner surfaces of its jaws, a dental arrangement more typical of filter‑feeding or suction‑feeding organisms than of early reptiles, which generally exhibit larger, conical teeth suited for grasping prey on land. These traits collectively point to a creature that likely inhabited shallow marine environments or brackish lagoons, feeding on small invertebrates or plankton rather than hunting terrestrial insects.

The reinterpretation carries significant implications for the broader narrative of vertebrate evolution during the Carboniferous period, a time of dramatic ecological diversification. If the fossil is not a reptile, the earliest unequivocal evidence for amniotes in the fossil record must be pushed forward, narrowing the window for when vertebrates first conquered land. Moreover, the discovery highlights a previously underappreciated diversity of early tetrapod-like organisms that retained aquatic adaptations well into the age of the first true reptiles. It suggests that the transition from water to land was not a single, linear event but a mosaic of experiments, with many lineages exploring semi‑aquatic lifestyles before committing fully to terrestrial life.

Experts caution that the reclassification does not diminish the specimen’s scientific value; rather, it enriches our understanding of the complex ecosystems that flourished in the late Devonian and early Carboniferous. “This fossil reminds us that the fossil record is a puzzle with pieces that can change shape as new technologies emerge,” said Dr. Elena Martínez, a vertebrate paleontologist not involved in the study. “Each revision forces us to refine our models of how major groups originated and interacted.”

The breakthrough underscores the growing role of non‑destructive imaging in paleontology, where traditional preparation can be risky or impossible. As synchrotron facilities become more accessible and scanning techniques improve, researchers anticipate a wave of re‑examinations of classic specimens, potentially rewriting other entrenched narratives in deep time. For now, the Scottish fossil stands as a vivid illustration of how modern tools can peel back the layers of history, revealing that even well‑studied fossils may still hold unexpected secrets.
